items.question: Examine the character and significance of the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) in Andhra, with reference to the Chirala–Perala, Pedanandipadu and Palnadu satyagrahas.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22)** turned Andhra — especially **Guntur, Krishna and Palnadu** — into one of the most active theatres of Gandhian mass politics in the Madras Presidency. Its character was **broad-based and largely non-violent**, drawing in peasants, small-town residents and forest-dwellers alongside the Congress intelligentsia, and combining **no-revenue satyagrahas, anti-liquor picketing, boycott of courts and councils, and the surrender of titles**.

The **Chirala–Perala satyagraha (1921)**, led by **Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya ('Andhra Ratna')**, saw the residents of the twin towns **abandon their homes** rather than pay enhanced municipal taxes, living for about eleven months in a hut-settlement called **Ramnagar** — a striking demonstration of collective non-cooperation. The **Pedanandipadu campaign** in Guntur, organised by **Parvataneni Veerayya Choudary** under the guidance of **Konda Venkatappayya ('Desabhakta')**, became the centre of a **no-revenue (no-tax) satyagraha** by the peasantry. In the **Palnadu forest satyagraha**, **Kanneganti Hanumanthu** led defiance of the **Pullari (grazing) tax** and forest restrictions, and was **shot dead in 1922**, becoming a martyr of the movement.

The **significance** of these episodes lies in the way they **fused economic grievances (taxes, forest and grazing rights) with the national cause**, deepened Congress's rural roots, and produced a generation of Andhra leaders and a distinct regional idiom of protest. Though suspended nationally after **Chauri Chaura (Feb 1922)**, the movement left an organisational and emotional base that sustained later Civil Disobedience, Quit India and the demand for a separate Andhra.
keyPoints: Non-Cooperation (1920–22) was strongest in Guntur, Krishna and Palnadu; broad-based and non-violent.
Chirala–Perala (1921): Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya led the exodus to 'Ramnagar' against municipal taxes.
Pedanandipadu (Guntur): no-revenue satyagraha by Parvataneni Veerayya Choudary, mentored by Konda Venkatappayya.
Palnadu: Kanneganti Hanumanthu led the Pullari/forest satyagraha and was martyred in 1922.
Significance: fused economic grievances with the national cause; deepened rural Congress base.
Suspended nationally after Chauri Chaura (Feb 1922) but seeded later movements.

items.question: "The Rampa Rebellion of 1922–24 was as much a tribal revolt against colonial forest policy as it was a nationalist uprising." Discuss with reference to Alluri Sitarama Raju.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Rampa (Manyam) Rebellion of 1922–24**, led by **Alluri Sitarama Raju** in the **Godavari agency**, sits at the intersection of **tribal grievance and nationalist resistance**, and both strands are essential to understanding it.

As a **tribal revolt**, its roots lay in colonial forest policy: the **1882 Madras Forest Act** and the reserved-forest regime **curtailed the hill tribes' podu (shifting) cultivation** and access to forest produce, while **forced, unpaid labour (vetti/begar)** on roads embittered the community. The revolt was thus a direct response to the **loss of customary livelihood and dignity** — a classic tribal uprising against the colonial appropriation of forests.

As a **nationalist uprising**, Raju — revered as **'Manyam Veerudu'** — infused the movement with the **anti-British ethos of the age**. Emerging soon after the Non-Cooperation phase, it channelled tribal anger into a wider **rejection of British authority**, using **guerrilla tactics** and **raids on police stations (Chintapalle, Krishnadevipeta, Rajavommangi)** to seize arms. The colonial state answered with the **Malabar Special Police**, and the rebellion ended with Raju's **capture and killing on 7 May 1924**.

The episode's importance lies in this **dual character**: it exposed the human cost of colonial forest laws, showed how **local, subaltern grievances could merge with the national struggle**, and gave Andhra one of its most enduring symbols of sacrifice. Unlike the Gandhian, non-violent campaigns elsewhere in Andhra, it represented the **armed, agrarian-tribal face** of the freedom movement.
keyPoints: Rampa/Manyam Rebellion (1922–24) led by Alluri Sitarama Raju in the Godavari agency.
Tribal cause: 1882 Madras Forest Act curbed podu cultivation and forest access; vetti (forced labour).
Nationalist cause: anti-British revolt using guerrilla raids on police stations for arms.
British used the Malabar Special Police; Raju captured and shot on 7 May 1924.
Dual character — subaltern forest grievance fused with the national struggle.
Represented the armed, agrarian-tribal face of Andhra's freedom movement, distinct from Gandhian satyagraha.
items.source: Wikipedia — Rampa Rebellion of 1922; Alluri Sitarama Raju

items.question: Assess the contribution of Andhra leaders to the national freedom struggle from the Vandemataram movement to Quit India.
items.modelAnswer:
From the **Vandemataram agitation** to **Quit India**, Andhra contributed leaders who gave the freedom struggle **regional depth and a distinctive character** across its every phase.

In the **Swadeshi/Vandemataram phase (1905–07)**, inspired by **Bipin Chandra Pal's 1907 tour**, figures such as **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** (jailed for sedition, an early Andhra political prisoner) carried extremist nationalism into the region, while the strongman **Kodi Rammurthy Naidu** became a symbol of **national self-confidence**. The **Home Rule Movement (1916)** then spread self-government ideas through the Madras Presidency.

The **Non-Cooperation era (1920–22)** produced Andhra's most celebrated leaders: **Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya ('Andhra Ratna')** of the Chirala–Perala satyagraha and first Andhra AICC secretary; **Konda Venkatappayya ('Desabhakta')**, organiser of district campaigns; **Parvataneni Veerayya Choudary** of the Pedanandipadu no-tax campaign; and **Kanneganti Hanumanthu**, martyr of the Palnadu forest satyagraha. The **poet Garimella Satyanarayana** mobilised the masses with patriotic songs and was repeatedly jailed. Simultaneously, **Alluri Sitarama Raju** led the armed **Rampa Rebellion (1922–24)**, adding a tribal-agrarian militancy.

In **Civil Disobedience (1930)**, **Tanguturi Prakasam ('Andhra Kesari')** — famed for baring his chest before the **Simon Commission (1928)** — and others led coastal salt satyagraha, and the tradition of mass mobilisation continued into the **Quit India Movement (1942)** with hartals, sabotage and arrests.

Collectively, Andhra's leaders supplied the movement with **oratory, poetry, peasant and tribal mobilisation, and organisational skill**, and their regional pride fed naturally into the later demand for a separate Andhra — making the province a vigorous and creative partner in the national struggle.
keyPoints: Swadeshi phase: Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao (sedition prisoner); Kodi Rammurthy Naidu (national self-confidence); Bipin Pal's 1907 tour.
Non-Cooperation: Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya (Andhra Ratna), Konda Venkatappayya (Desabhakta), Parvataneni Veerayya Choudary, Kanneganti Hanumanthu (Palnadu martyr).
Garimella Satyanarayana mobilised the masses with patriotic songs; jailed repeatedly.
Alluri Sitarama Raju led the armed Rampa Rebellion (1922–24), a tribal-agrarian strand.
Civil Disobedience: Tanguturi Prakasam (Andhra Kesari), Simon Commission defiance (1928), coastal salt satyagraha.
Andhra contributed oratory, poetry, peasant/tribal mobilisation and organisation; fed into the later separate-Andhra demand.
items.source: Wikipedia — Bipin Chandra Pal; Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya; Konda Venkatappayya; Alluri Sitarama Raju; Tanguturi Prakasam; Garimella Satyanarayana
